newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela to issue new lending guidelines - reports.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela to issue new lending guidelines - reports.

text.p: Venezuela's banking superintendency Sudeban, taken aback by a recent rise in lending, will shortly issue new industry guidelines to beef up loan provisions and bank control, local papers reported Tuesday.
"There is always a risk when lending begins again," Sudeban head Francisco Debera said, leading daily El Universal reported.
Sudeban is to shortly issue new guidelines requiring higher bad loan provisions after lending increased nearly 16 percent over the first quarter of the year, according to Sudeban figures.
That is a galloping increase by any standard but especially steep for Venezuela's banks, still fresh from the recovery room after nearly half the system collapsed in a 1994-5 banking crisis.
"We're aware that many banks have not kept up the required supervision of their credit departments after dedicating themselves to investing in TEMs for so long," said Debera.
Over the past two years of recession and restrained borrowing, as much as half the assets of Venezuela's liquidity rich banks have been invested in Central Bank bills, called TEMs.
The high yielding, low-risk paper has helped banks rebuild their balance sheets after the financial crisis swallowed an estimated $11 billion in bailouts.

But it also left banks' lending habit to wither, according to industry analysts, just as half the sector has been taken over by foreign banks -- so boosting competition in a hitherto relatively closed industry.
And as banks now shed TEMs for loans, it has also dented risk-adjusted capitalization rates, now standing at 11.37 percent, according to Sudeban.
Debera added that despite the new guidelines, the onus would remain with banks to conduct their operations safely and prudently.
"What really counts is that banks conduct their operations correctly," he said, financial daily Economia Hoy reported.
